doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

title: Playing on thousands of records he cannot recall
summary: At his peak he did fifteen sessions a week and cannot recognize much of it; hits are remembered, most records vanished.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: But the way the business works is just like Bucky Pizzarelli told me these funny stories about John had to tell him that he played on certain songs.
You know because he just did so much of that that he wouldn’t recognize –
That was the same with me. I mean at the height of my career I was playing fifteen recording sessions a week, and arranging three jingles. Like I was just so bus—I was

either writing or in the studio, and sometimes like I said you’d play tracks and you wouldn’t hear the vocal, you wouldn’t hear the song, I wouldn’t be able to recognize half, you know over half the stuff I played on. Soundtracks from movies and things like that, you know, how would you know?

No. I enjoyed it. It was challenging and it was stressful. Like I said, I always lived in the fear, my biggest fear was they’re going to find out that I’m not as good as they think I am. That was probably my biggest fear.
Well if I went down your list of recording credits on whatever website it was.

A discography, page after page after page and it’s probably incomplete but we might assume that the big names that pop out, you know three of the four Beatles and other names like that might have been the most memorable sessions for you. Is that necessarily true?

Yeah, yeah. Because those people were, those records were visible. You were going to hear them all the time everywhere. So those things you remember. But I probably played on 80% of the stuff that never saw the light of day. That was the other thing. People say, “Oh you played on this hit record, you played on that hit record.” Yeah but thousands of records you play on never see the light of day. You don’t remember them and they never went anywhere. You think about how many – the percentage of people that have hit records – it’s like winning the lottery. So most of the things you do you don’t remember.
And you don’t necessarily ever hear them again either.
I never hear them again, yeah, yeah.
